title: Anthropic's Lance Martin: 1,000 Claude Agents Formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 Hours, Build Their Own Memory
summary: 1,000 Claude agents formalized Fermat's last theorem in 30 hours and built memory
detailed: An Anthropic experiment using 1,000 Claude helper agents and one lead agent formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean within 30 hours without human intervention.
The lead agent autonomously created four SQL database tables to manage announcements, worker roles, progress notes, and verified code without being instructed to do so.
Anthropic researcher Lance Martin presented the results at the AI Engineer conference, contrasting this autonomous setup with a September run that required a dozen agents and a human-guided harness.
The experiment highlights that advanced AI agents can dynamically invent necessary operational primitives and effectively manage complex collaborative workflows.
sentences: Five minutes into a run that would last about 30 hours, the lead agent in an Anthropic experiment did something nobody told it to do.
One to broadcast announcements to the team, one to assign worker roles, one to share progress notes, and one — labeled "land" — to mark which pieces of Lean code had actually been verified.
Then it set 999 helper agents loose.

The result, described by Anthropic researcher Lance Martin at the AI Engineer conference, was a full formalization of Andrew Wiles' proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean, the proof-verification language.
No domain-specific orchestration platform.
No human steering on the mathematics.
Just Git, a SQL database, and a thousand Claude instances each running in its own sandbox with restricted network access.
"We are able to show this formalization, which was expected to take many, many years," Martin said.
Wiles himself spent seven years producing the original proof in the mid-1990s.
The headline number matters because of what it replaced.

In September, Anthropic reported that Claude had formalized the same proof — but that run used about a dozen agents, a purpose-built orchestration harness called "Prove to Me," and substantial hand-holding from a human researcher.
The new experiment, run alongside the Fable 5 model launch, stripped all of that away.
The prompt was minimal: it named the lead, the helpers, the two available tools, and the problem statement.
Most of the surrounding infrastructure, Martin said, was safety and security — real-time monitoring of every tool call for escapes, plus offline review of all agent runs every ten minutes.
The tables the lead agent invented are the story.
Martin's visualization shows the lead writing to the announce table only occasionally, while helpers continuously read and write to the notes and land tables.
"Agents now are sufficiently advanced that they can actually build primitives that they need to solve hard problems," he said.

"We didn't tell them to build these tables."
For the hardest sub-results — Martin cites Lagrange's theorem — the agents constructed their own task trees tracking dependencies and progress from in-progress to done, then reallocated themselves across the 60 proof statements as work completed.

One agent's note, which Martin quoted, reads: "total freeze of the origin, effective now, magnificent work all 999 of you."
The formalization result occupies the first half of Martin's talk.
The second half is about something less photogenic and arguably more consequential: how agents remember.
Martin frames it through Kierkegaard.
"Life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards," he said.

"This is a fundamental paradox of agent memory." Agents write memories myopically, judging what matters for the task in front of them, but memory has to be a coherent, non-redundant map the agent can later reason over.
The human analogy is the hippocampus recording daily experience and replaying it to the neocortex during sleep, consolidating the important fragments into long-term knowledge.
Anthropic found agents benefit from the same split — in-session writing, offline consolidation — and gave the offline step a name: dreaming.
On CL Bench, an open-source continual-learning benchmark, Claude gets 40 sequential questions about a database, each in a fresh session, with a memory directory it may write to between sessions.
The instruction is deliberately bare: the directory is there, use it if you want.

Stronger models, Martin said, write higher-quality memories — verified statements or predictions about database state rather than low-value observations — and know intrinsically when to retrieve them.
"Better models have much better instincts for salience and what to write to memory," he said.
"And you can see this reflected in the size of the memory directories.

It's much tighter, it's much more strategic."
The sharpest illustration comes from Pokémon.
Claude 3.7 and Fable 5 were each handed a memory directory and free rein to write whatever they wanted.
Claude 3.7 produced a sprawling, indiscriminate mess — Martin's word for it was "disgusting" — stuffed with experiences irrelevant to strategic play, and it progressed poorly.
Fable 5's directory was far smaller and tighter, holding strategic insights and tactical knowledge that cannot simply be read off the game state.
In Martin's visualization, box size encodes file count, making the contrast immediate.
Knowing what deserves to be written down is not a prompting trick; it is a capability that appears to scale with the model.
Memory has a failure mode that is worse than forgetting: remembering something wrong.
In one Pokémon run, Claude wrote down the wrong location of a landmark.
That poisoned note sent it into a loop — it mislocalized itself, fell through a trap door, and got returned to the prior level.
In trajectories where dreaming was applied, the raw-memory runs regress at that point while dreaming runs recover and advance.
"A poisoned memory was injected and it's stuck there.
Dreaming can rescue that," Martin said.

"That's really the intuition on why dreaming is extremely powerful for reflecting over memories and correcting them."
Dreaming works by having Claude reflect over transcripts and written notes and re-represent them: building wikis, promoting certain memories into context injected preemptively into every future session, and correcting errors.
Transcripts are the foundation of memory — plain transcript search is the naive baseline — but only a tiny fraction of their content is salient.
Anthropic tested this on a corpus from Stainless, a company it acquired in May, anonymized into a dataset.
It built 25 questions answerable only from that corpus — documents and Slack messages — then compared a semantic search baseline against letting Claude build a wiki from the material.
The wiki improved steadily as more dreaming tokens were spent, and the wiki combined with the search tool beat either alone.

Illustrative scale: the raw semantic-search baseline sits at roughly 53%, and wiki quality climbs as more dreaming compute is allocated; combining the wiki with the search tool outperforms either alone.
Source: Lance Martin, AI Engineer.
"As you add more dreaming compute, the wiki gets more and more useful," Martin said.

"We think this is a really nice mental model to think about how agents can build knowledge over time."
A second example shows dreaming repairing a wiki directly.
Before dreaming, Claude's wiki contained placeholder pages for entries that did not exist.
After dreaming, it filled many gaps and generated an index.
Martin lists three jobs for dreaming compute: correcting mistakes, filling knowledge gaps, and creating new representations such as wikis.
Look at the two halves together and they point one direction.
In September, multi-agent work required a hand-built harness and a researcher in the loop; by the thousand-agent run, the agents had built their own coordination layer in a database within minutes.
In memory, explicit prompting was unnecessary for stronger models — they decide on their own when to write and read.
In both cases, the demonstrated capability is the model supplying structure that engineers previously had to supply.
The obvious caution is generalization.
The formalization is a single run on a problem with a machine-checkable success criterion — Lean either verifies the code or it does not.
